I will use the randomized public lottery that assigned districts to fiber construction phases (fiber_phase) as an instrument for household broadband subscription share, estimating local average treatment effects of broadband on 11th-grade test scores via two-stage least squares: first stage regressing broadband share on phase indicators (and crew_order for phase-3 variation), second stage regressing test scores on predicted broadband share. Key variables: treatment = district household broadband subscription share (percentage points), outcome = district average 11th-grade standardized test score, instruments = fiber_phase (1–4) and crew_order (months within phase 3) to capture exogenous timing of backbone arrival that the program documentation says mechanically changed subscription rates. I will include baseline covariates (median_income, rural_share, per_pupil, college_share, enroll) to improve precision and control for any residual imbalances from the lottery; standard errors clustered at the county/district grouping used for the lottery if applicable. The main identification assumption is that phase assignment and crew order affect test scores only through changes in household broadband (exclusion restriction), conditional on controls and given the randomized lottery; a main threat is that the fiber grant also funded school computer labs at the start of each district’s phase, which creates a direct channel to test scores and would violate the exclusion restriction unless I can separately control for lab deployment or use variation in crew_order (which affected subscription timing but not the grant-funded labs) to isolate broadband exposure timing. I will test instrument relevance (first-stage F-statistic) and examine balance on pre-treatment outcomes and covariates across phases and crew_order to probe possible violations.  
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
dist_datacenter | doubtful
median_income | violated
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

I will use the randomized phasing and crew-order lotteries as instruments for district household broadband share to estimate the causal effect on 11th-grade test scores via two-stage least squares: first stage regresses broadband subscription share on fiber_phase (coded 1–4) and, for the phase-3 subsample, crew_order (0–11) and their interactions with phase indicators to capture differential timing; second stage regresses mean 11th-grade test score on predicted broadband share. Key variables: outcome = district average 11th-grade standardized test score (2014), endogenous treatment = share of households with broadband subscription (percentage points), instruments = fiber_phase and crew_order (for phase-3 districts), controls = baseline district covariates such as median_income, rural_share, per_pupil, college_share, enroll, and county fixed effects to improve precision and account for geographic confounders. The main identifying assumption is that the lotteries affected test scores only through changes in household broadband (exclusion), but potential violations include direct effects of the grant-funded school computer labs or concurrent timing of other interventions correlated with phase assignment; I will test for balance on observables across phases and for first-stage strength, and use the computer-lab funding timing (available from program memo and facili_* variables) as a robustness check and, if needed, control or instrument validity probe. Heterogeneity checks: IV estimates within phase strata and checks excluding districts with early/late data-entry anomalies; sensitivity to controlling for facili_* (facility/computer-lab) measures and to excluding districts with small N (privacy-suppressed) will assess robustness. Main threat: violation of exclusion due to the program also funding in-school computer labs and other services that directly affect test scores contemporaneously with broadband arrival.  
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
facili_shar_070 | violated
facili_date_017 | doubtful
median_income | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

I will exploit the quasi-random phasing lottery for the state-subsidized fiber backbone as an instrumental-variables design: fiber_phase (1–4) — and within phase 3, the crew_order lottery (months 0–11) — plausibly randomized assignments that affected district household broadband subscription shares in 2014 but did not directly set test scores except through broadband and the small computer-lab build funded at phase arrival. The endogenous treatment is district-level broadband_share (share of households with a broadband subscription, in percentage points) and the outcome is the district average 11th-grade standardized test score in 2014; I will estimate first-stage regressions of broadband_share on fiber_phase (and crew_order for phase-3 districts), controlling flexibly for baseline covariates (median_income, rural_share, per_pupil, college_share, enroll) and county fixed effects, then the second-stage IV estimate of test score on predicted broadband_share. I will run balance tests of pre-treatment covariates by phase and crew_order, and use weak-instrument diagnostics, clustered standard errors at the county or district level, and sensitivity checks excluding districts that received computer-lab investments contemporaneously to assess direct treatment of schooling resources. The main threat is that the fiber-phase assignment or crew arrival timing may have affected test scores through channels other than household broadband (e.g., district-level infrastructure grants, timing of computer-lab installation, or other correlated state supports), violating the exclusion restriction; I will test this by controlling for observable contemporaneous district investments and by estimating effects in subsamples with and without lab installation. If exclusion looks violated, I will report reduced-form intent-to-treat effects of fiber_phase and crew_order on test scores instead of IV causal effects.  
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
dist_datacenter | doubtful
median_income | violated
college_share | violated
per_pupil | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

I will use the lottery-like phasing and within-phase crew-order as instruments in a two-stage least squares (2SLS) IV design that leverages exogenous variation from the public lottery assignment (fiber_phase) and randomized crew arrival timing (crew_order) to predict 2014 district broadband subscription share and estimate its effect on 11th-grade average test scores. Key variables: treatment = district household broadband subscription share in 2014 (continuous, percentage points); outcome = district average 11th-grade standardized test score in 2014; instruments = fiber_phase (ordinal 1–4) and crew_order (0–11 months, for phase-3 districts); controls = baseline covariates like median_income, rural_share, per_pupil, college_share, enroll to improve precision and account for residual imbalance. Identification assumption: the instruments affect test scores only through their impact on household broadband subscription share (exclusion) and are as-good-as-random due to the public lottery and internal random ordering, conditional on controls. I will test instrument strength (first-stage F-stat) and perform balance checks on pre-treatment covariates across phase and crew-order, plus placebo tests using outcomes that should not respond (e.g., pre-2011 scores or lagged outcomes if available). Main threat: the state program also triggered contemporaneous transfers (the fixed annual technology fund disbursement to connected districts) and possible hardware or school-level investments correlated with fiber_phase timing, which can violate exclusion by providing direct schooling resources that affect test scores independent of household broadband; I will attempt to control for observable program transfers if measurable and interpret estimates as the combined effect of increased household broadband plus any direct program effects if not separable. 
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
dist_datacenter | doubtful
median_income | violated
popula_coun_003 | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

I will use the randomized public lottery that assigned districts to fiber construction phases (fiber_phase) and, within phase 3, the crew_order lottery as instruments for district household broadband subscription share to implement a two-stage least squares (2SLS) IV design estimating the effect of a one percentage-point increase in broadband subscriptions on 11th-grade average test scores. Key variables: outcome = district average 11th-grade standardized test score (2014), treatment = share of households with a broadband subscription (percentage points, 2014), instruments = fiber_phase (coded 1–4) and crew_order (0–11, for phase-3 districts), controls = pre-treatment covariates such as median_income, rural_share, college_share, per_pupil, and enroll to improve precision and account for any residual imbalance. The first stage will confirm that later phases and later crew arrival mechanically lowered 2014 subscription shares by about 4.0 and 1.0 percentage points per phase/month respectively (as documented), and the second stage will estimate the local average treatment effect for districts whose broadband status was shifted by the lotteries. I will cluster standard errors at the district level, report weak-instrument diagnostics (F-statistics) and overidentification tests where applicable, and show balance tests of pre-treatment covariates across instrument values. The main threat is noncompliance of private ISPs or differential concurrent interventions (e.g., the state school technology fund disbursements tied to being on the connected list) that the lottery also affects, which would violate the exclusion restriction by creating direct effects on test scores aside from household broadband uptake. To probe this, I will run placebo outcomes and control for receipt of the fixed state disbursement and, if the exclusion restriction remains doubtful, present bounds and intent-to-treat estimates by instrumented assignment instead of subscription share.
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
median_income | doubtful
rural_share | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

Estimate an instrumental-variables (IV) local-average-treatment-effect using the randomized phasing lottery (fiber_phase) as the instrument for district household broadband share to capture exogenous variation in access caused by the state's staged rollout. Key variables: instrument = fiber_phase (1–4, each phase later reduces 2014 broadband share by ~4 pp); treatment = district share of households with a broadband subscription (percentage points, 2014); outcome = district average 11th-grade standardized test score (2014); control for pre-treatment covariates (median_income, rural_share, college_share, per_pupil, enroll) to improve precision and check balance. Use two-stage least squares where first stage regresses broadband share on fiber_phase (and crew_order as an additional instrument for within-phase timing among phase-3 districts in robustness checks), and second stage regresses test scores on the predicted broadband share; cluster SEs at an appropriate geographic level (county/district) and report first-stage F-stat. Main threat: violations of the exclusion restriction if fiber_phase also affects test scores through other channels (e.g., contemporaneous program payments, state fund disbursements, or differential timing of related school investments tied to the connected-districts list). I will test this by showing that pre-treatment outcomes and trends do not vary by phase, by including variables for the state technology fund disbursements or timing if available, and by running placebo outcomes and crew_order-only IV in phase-3.  
CANDIDATES:
fiber_phase | plausible
crew_order | plausible
dist_datacenter | doubtful
median_income | violated
INSTRUMENT: fiber_phase

I will exploit the discontinuities created by the 40-student cap and the ministry's staffing rule: use rule_size (predicted class size from grade enrollment divided by the number of classes the cap requires) as an instrument for actual class size in a two-stage least squares (2SLS) framework, controlling flexibly for a smooth function of enroll_grade and clustering SEs by school. Key variables: treatment = actual class size, instrument = rule_size, outcome = class average reading score, controls = polynomial in enroll_grade (or enroll counts) and baseline prior_score plus school fixed effects and pct_disadv, town_size, religious, teacher_exp. The first stage leverages discrete jumps in rule_size when enrollment crosses 40, 80, 120 to generate exogenous variation in class size (a one-student change in predicted size lowers actual size by 0.7 students per ministry memo). I will test instrument strength (F-stat), check for balance of observed covariates around enrollment thresholds, and estimate local average treatment effects for compliers. Main threat: manipulation of enrollment counts or class reporting around the thresholds (e.g., strategic class formation or misreporting) that would invalidate the exclusion restriction by correlating rule_size with unobserved determinants of test scores. I will address this threat with McCrary density tests at cutpoints and robustness checks excluding observations within small windows around discontinuities.
CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
split_audit | doubtful
enroll_grade | violated
INSTRUMENT: rule_size

I will use a fuzzy regression discontinuity design exploiting the 40-student cap: predicted class size (rule_size), which jumps discretely when grade enrollment crosses multiples of 40, as an instrument for actual class size to estimate its effect on class average reading score via two-stage least squares, controlling flexibly for a smooth function of enrollment and clustering SEs by school. Key variables: outcome = class average reading score; endogenous treatment = actual class size; instrument = rule_size (predicted size from enrollment and required number of classes); running variable = enroll_grade with polynomial/linear controls and bandwidth chosen by cross-validation and robustness checks. I will check first-stage strength (rule_size → actual size) and continuity of baseline covariates (pct_disadv, prior_score, teacher_exp, town_size, religious, split_audit) at the enrollment cutoffs, and perform placebo cutoffs and alternative bandwidths. I will also estimate local average treatment effects and report bounds and sensitivity to functional-form choices. The main threat is manipulation of enrollment counts or sorting around multiples of 40 (or violations of exclusion if the cap affects other inputs like remedial reading-hours grant correlated with outcomes). To mitigate, I will test for bunching in enroll_grade and control for any policy-induced grants (using administrative indicators) and report results excluding audited schools.  
CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
split_audit | doubtful
enroll_grade | violated
pct_disadv | doubtful
prior_score | doubtful
teacher_exp | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: rule_size

I will use a regression-discontinuity (RD) design exploiting the kinks in the rule_size schedule created by the 40-student cap (predicted class size drops when grade enrollment crosses 40, 80, 120) to identify the causal effect of actual class size on class-average reading scores, controlling for a smooth polynomial in enroll_grade and clustering standard errors by school. Key variables: outcome = class average reading score; treatment = actual class size; running variable = enroll_grade (or rule_size as the derived predicted size) with cutoffs at multiples of 40; controls = smooth functions of enroll_grade and pct_disadv, town_size, religious, teacher_exp, prior_score to improve precision. I will implement local linear RD around each enrollment threshold and/or a kink RD using the continuous predicted-size rule to exploit changes in the slope of predicted size, test for manipulation of enrollments, and check robustness to bandwidth choice and higher-order polynomials. I will cluster inference at the school level and report McCrary density tests and placebo cutoffs to assess validity. The main threat is local nonrandom sorting or manipulation of enrollments around the thresholds (or differential implementation of the cap) that would invalidate the continuity assumption. I will pre-register bandwidth and specification choices and conduct falsification checks using pre-treatment outcomes and variables unlikely to be affected by class size.

CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
enroll_grade | plausible
split_audit | doubtful
pct_disadv | violated
INSTRUMENT: NONE

I will use a regression discontinuity design (RDD) exploiting the staffing rule that caps class size at 40 by forcing the number of classes (and thus predicted class size, rule_size) to jump discretely when grade enrollment crosses multiples of 40, estimating the local causal effect of actual class size on class-average reading scores using classes near those enrollment cutoffs. The running variable is enroll_grade (or equivalently rule_size as constructed from enroll_grade and the ministry’s required number-of-classes), the treatment is actual class size, and the outcome is class average reading score; I will control flexibly for a smooth polynomial in enroll_grade and cluster standard errors by school. I will implement both "sharp"/"fuzzy" RDD specifications as needed because the cap induces a change in predicted size while actual size responds imperfectly (the memo notes a 0.7 student actual change per one-student change in predicted size), instrumenting actual size with the discontinuity in rule_size for a fuzzy RDD. I will check validity with McCrary density tests at the enrollment multiples, covariate balance of pre-determined class/school variables (prior_score, pct_disadv, teacher_exp, town_size, religious), and robustness to bandwidth and polynomial order. The main threat is manipulation or sorting of enrollments around the cutoffs (or other institutional responses correlated with crosses of the 40-student thresholds) that would invalidate the local randomization assumption. If manipulation is detected or the discontinuity is weak, I will not use the RDD and will report NONE. 

CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
enroll_grade | plausible
split_audit | doubtful
pct_disadv | violated
prior_score | violated
INSTRUMENT: rule_size

I will use a fuzzy regression discontinuity exploiting the staffing rule that caps classes at 40 students: predicted class size (rule_size) jumps discontinuously when grade enrollment crosses multiples of 40 because the ministry requires additional classes, and this induces plausibly exogenous variation in actual class size (treatment) while class-average reading score is the outcome. Key variables: outcome = class average reading score, treatment = actual class size, running variable = enroll_grade (or predicted size rule_size), and instrument/forcing indicator = the discontinuous step in rule_size at enrollment thresholds; control for a smooth polynomial in enrollment and cluster SEs by school. I will estimate the local average treatment effect using two-stage least squares where the first stage regresses actual class size on the discontinuity-based instrument (e.g., indicator for enrollment just above each multiple-of-40 threshold or the predicted class size from the rule) and the second stage regresses reading scores on predicted class size; bandwidth selection and robustness to polynomial order will be reported. The main threat is manipulation of enrollment around the thresholds (sorting) or other concurrent policy changes at those enrollment cutoffs that differentially affect test scores; I will test for bunching and balance of covariates (pct_disadv, prior_score, town_size, religious, teacher_exp, split_audit, etc.) around the cutoffs to assess this. If manipulation is detected, I will switch to using the random 1991 audit draw (split_audit) as an alternative instrument in an IV design, since audited grades were assigned one extra class exogenously and are reported to have only changed class size. I will cluster standard errors at the school level and report first-stage F-statistics and local randomization checks.

CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
split_audit | plausible
enroll_grade | doubtful
pct_disadv | violated
prior_score | violated
teacher_exp | violated
INSTRUMENT: rule_size

I will use a regression discontinuity design exploiting the nonlinearity in rule_size induced by the 40-student cap: predicted class size (rule_size) jumps down discretely when grade enrollment crosses multiples of 40, which plausibly creates exogenous variation in actual class size (treatment) around those cutoffs while controlling for a smooth function of enroll_grade. The key variables are actual class size (treatment), class average reading score (outcome), rule_size as the running variable (constructed from enroll_grade and number of classes implied by the cap), and prior_score plus pct_disadv, town_size, religious, and teacher_exp as covariates to improve precision; I will cluster standard errors by school and use local polynomial estimators with bandwidth selection and robustness checks. Identification assumes that crossing the enrollment thresholds affects outcomes only through class size (no other discrete changes at the same cutoffs), so I will test for manipulations of enrollments, discontinuities in baseline covariates, and the split_audit indicator as a falsification check. I will also estimate the first-stage relationship and report local average treatment effects for compliers, and run placebo cutoffs and varying bandwidths to assess robustness. The main threat is that other policies or resource rules (e.g., the remedial reading-hours grant or administrative staffing/budget changes) also change discretely at the same enrollment thresholds and thus violate the exclusion restriction. CANDIDATES:
rule_size | plausible
split_audit | doubtful
enroll_grade | violated
budget_most_010 | doubtful
staffi_most_101 | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: rule_size

I will estimate the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of assignment to being offered services (assigned) on total earnings in the 30 months after random assignment using randomized assignment within sites plus site fixed effects as the primary identification strategy, exploiting the original randomization (two-thirds offered, one-third barred) to ensure unconfoundedness. Key variables are assigned (treatment assignment indicator), earn30 (total earnings in 30 months; create or use the documented earnings outcome variable from codebook fields such as earnin_amou_103 / earnin_most_030 / earnin_base_108 as appropriate to compose the 30-month total), site (site fixed effects), and baseline covariates (age, female, hs_grad, prior_earn, afdc, married) only to improve precision and check balance. Because take-up is incomplete, I will also report the local average treatment effect (LATE) using assignment as an instrument for enrollment (actual receipt/enrolled indicator) in a two-stage least squares (2SLS) framework, clustering standard errors at the site level to account for within-site correlation. I will pre-specify analyzing ITT as primary and complier LATE as secondary, include checks for differential attrition using follow-up flags and imputation indicators, and run subgroup heterogeneity by fast_track and baseline prior_earn. The main threat is post-randomization confounding from differential access to the state employment agency’s priority for subsidized public-sector jobs given to the offered group (an intentional non-treatment channel that could bias interpretation of program-service effects versus administrative-priority effects).  

CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | doubtful
enrolled | violated
prior_earn | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: assigned

I will estimate the ITT effect of being offered services on 30-month earnings using the randomized assignment indicator (assigned) as the primary instrument for actual enrollment/treatment (treatment = enrolled), implementing two-stage least squares with site fixed effects and baseline stratification by site to preserve randomization. Key variables: outcome = total earnings in the 30 months after random assignment (earnings variable as provided, deflated if nominal), treatment = enrollment indicator (enrolled), instrument = assigned, controls = baseline covariates (age, female, hs_grad, prior_earn, afdc, married) included only to improve precision and not for identification; include site fixed effects and robust standard errors clustered at site. I will report ITT (reduced form) and LATE (IV) estimates, check first-stage F-statistic, and present balance tests and heterogeneity by fast_track and baseline prior_earn to probe mechanisms. Main threat: noncompliance correlated with unobserved post-randomization administrative enrollment practices (e.g., fast-track scheduling or differential referral recording) that violate exclusion if they directly affect earnings aside from treatment. I will perform sensitivity checks excluding records with post-2014 vendor changes and using alternative earnings measures (e.g., wage-only) to assess robustness. If the exclusion restriction or first-stage fails, I will rely on ITT estimates only.

CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | doubtful
assigned × site indicators | violated
INSTRUMENT: assigned

I'll use the randomized offer (assigned) as the instrument for actual enrollment (treatment = enrolled in program services) and estimate local average treatment effects via two-stage least squares (first stage: enrolled = α + π·assigned + site fixed effects + ε; second stage: earnings30 = β + τ·enrolled_hat + site fixed effects + controls + u), leveraging random assignment within site to satisfy exclusion and independence. Key variables: assigned (random offer indicator, instrument), enrolled (actual treatment), earn30 (total earnings 30 months post-random assignment, outcome), site fixed effects (to account for within-site randomization), and baseline covariates like prior_earn, age, female, hs_grad, afdc, and married to improve precision. I will cluster standard errors at the site level to account for within-site correlation and report ITT (intent-to-treat) and IV LATE estimates; I will also show first-stage F-statistic and describe complier characteristics. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because the assigned indicator also granted first priority for state subsidized public-sector job openings (an independent programmatic benefit), which could directly affect earnings even absent enrollment. To probe this, I'll run sensitivity analyses excluding outcomes plausibly affected by the priority (e.g., public-sector wages if identifiable) and interact assigned with fast_track to test heterogeneity tied to scheduling-induced enrollment differences. If exclusion appears violated I will instead report ITT estimates by assigned and refrain from claiming causal effects of enrollment beyond the offer. 
CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | doubtful
enroll_date (traini_date_073) | violated
INSTRUMENT: assigned

I will estimate the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of being offered services on 30-month earnings using randomized assignment (assigned) as the primary source of identification and include site fixed effects to account for the within-site 2:1 randomization. Key variables: outcome = total earnings in 30 months (earnings variable, e.g., earnin_most_030 or earnin_amou_239 as appropriate), treatment indicator for enrollment (treatment = enrolled in program services if available) and assignment indicator (assigned) as the randomized offer. Because assignment was randomized and recorded for all applicants, the ITT estimate (difference in mean earnings between assigned=1 and assigned=0) provides a credible causal effect of offer; to estimate local average treatment effect (LATE) of enrollment I will use assigned as an instrument for actual enrollment in a two-stage least squares (2SLS) with site fixed effects and baseline covariates (age, female, hs_grad, prior_earn, afdc, married) to improve precision. I will cluster standard errors at the site level and check balance on baseline covariates and first-stage strength (F-stat) and report both ITT and IV estimates scaled by the first-stage. The main threat is post-randomization administrative selection or differential data linkage (missingness or delayed entries, or merged/hashed identifier issues) that could induce nonrandom measurement of earnings across assignment groups; I will test for differential missingness and robustness to alternative earnings measures and to excluding records with system-migration timing issues. If instrument validity or linkage problems persist, I will report ITT only and be transparent about data limitations.

CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | doubtful
earnin_date_052 | violated
INSTRUMENT: assigned

I will estimate the intention-to-treat (ITT) causal effect of being offered services on 30-month earnings using the randomized assignment "assigned" as the primary source of identification, exploiting random assignment within site and including site fixed effects; this provides a credible experiment-based estimate of offer effects and avoids post-treatment bias from enrollment. To learn about the effect of actual enrollment (treatment-on-treated, TOT), I will implement a two-stage least squares (2SLS) IV where first stage predicts enrollment using assignment (and fast_track as a secondary random encouragement instrument among the offered group), and the second stage estimates earnings on predicted enrollment; standard errors will be clustered at site. Key variables are earnin_amou_103 or the appropriate earnings total variable for 30 months as the outcome, assigned as the randomized instrument, and an observed enrollment indicator (treatment uptake) as the endogenous regressor; covariates (age, female, hs_grad, prior_earn, afdc, married) will be included to improve precision but not for identification. I will check randomization balance across baseline covariates by assigned and test for differential attrition in the earnings data by assigned to assess missingness as a threat; if attrition is related to assignment I will use inverse-probability weighting and bounds. The main threat is noncompliance correlated with unobserved characteristics that affect earnings (e.g., selective enrollment driven by motivation) and any differential linkage/missing earnings records by assignment that could bias IV estimates; therefore I will report ITT, IV (LATE), and sensitivity analyses to attrition and heterogeneous compliance. Pre-analysis will verify that fast_track is randomized only within the offered group and satisfies exclusion (affects earnings only via enrollment timing) before using it as a secondary instrument or otherwise treat it as an encouragement covariate.

CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | plausible
prior_earn | doubtful
age | doubtful
female | doubtful
hs_grad | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: assigned

Because treatment (offer of services) was randomized within site, I will estimate the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of being offered services on 30-month earnings using site fixed effects and randomization strata, and then recover the local average treatment effect (LATE) of enrollment using assignment as an instrument for actual enrollment (two-stage least squares). Key variables: assigned (instrument), treatment uptake/enrolled (first-stage endogenous treatment), and earnin_amou_103 or the appropriate earnings total variable for 30 months (outcome), with site indicators and baseline prior_earn, age, female, hs_grad, afdc, married as pre-specified precision covariates. I will cluster standard errors at the site level and check first-stage F-statistic and balance of covariates by assigned; I will also estimate ITT in subgroups (fast_track interaction) to probe heterogeneity. The main threat is differential measurement or missingness in the administrative earnings records correlated with assignment (e.g., barred applicants seeking services elsewhere or differential linkage/migration) that could bias ITT or violate the exclusion restriction for the instrument if assignment affects earnings through channels other than enrollment. I will run robustness checks restricting to records with high-quality linkage flags and assess sensitivity to excluding sites with large post-2013 data harmonization issues.

CANDIDATES:
assigned | plausible
fast_track | doubtful
prior_earn | violated
INSTRUMENT: assigned

I will use the ballot-draw as a randomized encouragement instrument for migration and estimate the local average treatment effect (LATE) of migrating within two years on weekly income three years after the ballot using two-stage least squares with ballot_drawn as the instrument for the binary treatment "migrated within two years" (first stage: migration ~ ballot_drawn + ballot-year fixed effects; second stage: income_three_years ~ predicted_migration + same fixed effects). Key variables: treatment = migrated within two years (constructed from travel/administrative dates), instrument = ballot_drawn, outcome = weekly income three years after the ballot (in NZD, CPI-deflated if necessary), and ballot-year fixed effects to account for changing quota sizes and macro conditions; include pre-ballot covariates (age, female, educ, employed_app, income_app, hh_size, househ_coun_000) only for precision. I will check the instrument strength (first-stage F-stat) and test balance of pre-ballot covariates by ballot_drawn to support randomization; I will also estimate ITT (reduced form) and report compliers interpretation. Main threat: violation of exclusion if being drawn affects income directly (e.g., through access to the training institute or being placed on the successful-applicant register) rather than only via migration; I will probe this by controlling for training participation and by using administrative markers of program exposure, and by sensitivity bounds. Robustness: heterogeneity by sex, baseline employment, and by fare_pilot status (which affects migration probability among drawn) and falsification checks using outcomes measured before migration.

CANDIDATES:
ballot_drawn | plausible
fare_pilot | doubtful
educ | doubtful
income_app | violated
INSTRUMENT: ballot_drawn

Because ballots are drawn at random each year, I will use an instrumental-variables (IV) approach that instruments individual migration within two years with ballot_drawn, estimating the effect of migration on weekly income three years after the ballot; include ballot-year fixed effects to account for time-varying selection into the draw. Key variables: treatment = migrated within two years (constructed from administrative visa/travel records), instrument = ballot_drawn, outcome = weekly income three years after the ballot (in NZD), and baseline covariates (age, female, educ, employed_app, income_app, hh_size, and relevant flags) to improve precision and check balance. I will estimate two-stage least squares (first stage: migrated ~ ballot_drawn + year FE + covariates; second stage: income ~ predicted_migrated + year FE + covariates) and report robust standard errors clustered at the ballot cohort if multiple draws per cohort. I will test instrument relevance (F-statistic) and perform balance checks on pre-ballot covariates and placebo outcomes to support the exclusion restriction. The main threat is that ballot_drawn affects income through channels other than migration (e.g., access to the successful-applicant register benefits like free training or administrative linkage differences), which would violate exclusion. To address this, I will control for receipt of training and check heterogeneity excluding those who never obtained a job offer or who did not access training, and I will present bounds and IV with additional controls as sensitivity analyses.
CANDIDATES:
ballot_drawn | plausible
fare_pilot | doubtful
income_app | violated
INSTRUMENT: ballot_drawn

Estimate a local average treatment effect (LATE) of migration on weekly income using the random ballot draw as an instrument for migrating within two years (IV: ballot_drawn → Treatment: migrated within two years → Outcome: weekly income three years after the ballot), including ballot-year fixed effects to account for any year-specific eligibility/quota shocks. Key variables: instrument = ballot_drawn; endogenous treatment = indicator for migrating within two years (constructed from administrative movement/visa records); outcome = income three years after the ballot (weekly NZD); covariates for precision only: age, female, educ, employed_app, income_app, hh_size and county/district fixed effects. Verify instrument validity by showing (a) strong first stage (draw raises migration probability ≈46 pp as documented) and (b) balance of pre-draw observables across drawn vs. not-drawn within ballot-year; report F-statistic and covariate balance tests. Main threat: noncompliance related to post-draw job-offer acquisition (drawn must still get a job offer), which could violate exclusion if the draw itself affects post-draw job-search resources or selection into job offers that also predict income; assess by testing whether drawn applicants were differentially enrolled or treated by the government training institute or received other supports (controls or subgroup IV on those without job-offer requirement). Conduct robustness: bounds/ATE sensitivity (e.g., monotonicity checks), IV with interaction by fare_pilot among drawn (as an encouragement to migrate) and estimate complier characteristics.  
CANDIDATES:
ballot_drawn | plausible
fare_pilot | doubtful
income_app | violated
age | violated
educ | violated
